specPoints.text: describe the structure of an atom in terms of protons, neutrons and electrons and use symbols such as 14 C to describe particular nuclei 6
know the terms atomic (proton) number, mass (nucleon) number and isotope

primer.text: Atoms hide almost all of their mass in a nucleus barely a ten-thousandth of their size. This note maps the three subatomic particles, shows why a neutral atom balances charge to zero, and teaches nuclear notation so any nucleus can be read as two numbers and a symbol.

lessons.title: The nucleus and its particles
lessons.opening: An atom is built from a tiny, dense nucleus holding protons and neutrons, with electrons orbiting far outside. The nucleus carries nearly all the mass; the electrons occupy almost all the volume, so most of the atom is empty space.
keyPoints: Atoms have a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and the nucleus is more than 10,000 times smaller still.
Protons sit in the nucleus with relative charge +1 and relative mass 1.
Neutrons also sit in the nucleus: no charge, relative mass 1.
Electrons orbit the nucleus with charge −1 and a negligible mass (about 1/2000 of a nucleon).
Almost the whole mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.

low.restatement: Draw an atom: a cramped central bundle of protons and neutrons, with much lighter electrons whizzing around a shell far away. The bundle carries nearly everything heavy.
low.analogy: The atom is like a stadium with a single pea on the centre spot — the pea is the nucleus and the stadium is where the electrons roam.
low.examPointer: Particle-property tables are near-certain marks: memorise charge +1/0/−1 and mass 1/1/negligible for proton, neutron, electron.

medium.restatement: The nucleus concentrates nucleons whose relative masses are each 1, so the atom’s mass is effectively the nucleon count. Electrons contribute charge balance but almost no mass, which is why chemical behaviour and nuclear identity are governed by different particle counts.
medium.analogy: Weigh a full bus (the nucleus) against the driver’s wristwatch (the electrons): the watch matters for timing, not for weight.
medium.examPointer: If a question compares nuclear and atomic radii, quote the factor of about 10,000 and state that the nucleus holds almost all of the mass.

check.stem: Where is nearly all of the mass of an atom concentrated?

options.text: in the nucleus
options.explanation: Protons and neutrons each carry relative mass 1 and both sit in the nucleus.

options.text: in the electron shells
options.explanation: Electrons have negligible mass, roughly 1/2000 of a nucleon.

options.text: spread evenly through the atom
options.explanation: Mass is concentrated, not spread — the nucleus is dense.

options.text: in the empty space between particles
options.explanation: The space holds no mass; it is simply volume.

check.stem: Which row correctly gives the relative charge and relative mass of a neutron?

options.text: charge 0, mass 1
options.explanation: A neutron carries no charge and has the same relative mass as a proton.

options.text: charge +1, mass 1
options.explanation: That describes a proton, not a neutron.

options.text: charge −1, mass negligible
options.explanation: That describes an electron.

options.text: charge 0, mass negligible
options.explanation: The neutron is heavy; only the electron has negligible mass.

check.stem: How large is an atom, compared with its nucleus?

options.text: the nucleus is more than 10,000 times smaller than the atom
options.explanation: The nucleus radius is tiny compared with the atomic radius.

options.text: the nucleus and atom are about the same size
options.explanation: The nucleus occupies a minute fraction of the atomic volume.

options.text: the nucleus is twice the radius of the atom
options.explanation: Nothing of the atom is larger than the atom itself.

options.text: the electrons orbit closer to the nucleus than its own radius
options.explanation: Electrons orbit well outside the nucleus.

check.stem: A lithium nucleus contains 3 protons and 4 neutrons. Where would you find the electrons of a neutral lithium atom?

options.text: orbiting the nucleus, 3 of them
options.explanation: Electrons orbit the nucleus; a neutral atom has electrons equal to protons (3).

options.text: inside the nucleus alongside the neutrons
options.explanation: Electrons never sit in the nucleus.

options.text: orbiting the nucleus, 4 of them
options.explanation: The electron count matches the proton count (3), not the neutron count.

options.text: bonded to the neutrons
options.explanation: Electrons are not bonded to neutrons; they orbit the nucleus.

check.stem: Why is most of an atom described as empty space?

options.text: because the electrons orbit at a distance from a nucleus that is minute compared with the atom
options.explanation: The volume is dominated by the orbital region, not the packed nucleus.

options.text: because atoms contain no matter at all
options.explanation: Atoms are matter — the particles are simply tiny and far apart.

options.text: because protons and neutrons have no mass
options.explanation: Nucleons each have relative mass 1.

options.text: because electrons fill the whole atom uniformly
options.explanation: Electrons occupy discrete orbitals, not a uniform fill.

check.stem: State the three subatomic particles and where each is found in an atom.
check.modelAnswer: Protons and neutrons are found in the nucleus, and electrons orbit around the nucleus.

check.stem: Give the relative charge and relative mass of an electron.
check.modelAnswer: An electron has a relative charge of −1 and a negligible relative mass of about 1/2000 of a nucleon.

check.stem: Explain why an atom is electrically neutral even though it contains charged particles.
check.modelAnswer: The number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the +1 charge of each proton is cancelled by the −1 charge of each electron, giving a total charge of zero.

check.stem: A neutral atom contains 4 neutrons and 3 electrons. State how many protons it has and the total charge of its nucleus.
check.modelAnswer: The atom is neutral, so protons equal electrons: 3 protons. The nucleus charge comes only from protons, so it is +3 (the 4 neutrons add no charge).

lessons.title: Charge, ions and nuclear notation
lessons.opening: Nuclear notation writes any nucleus as a symbol with two numbers: the mass number on top and the atomic number underneath. Reading those numbers tells you the protons, neutrons and electrons of the atom, and losing an electron turns the neutral atom into an ion.
keyPoints: The total charge of a neutral atom is zero because protons and electrons balance exactly.
An atom that loses electrons is ionised.
Nuclear notation places the mass number above and the atomic number below the element symbol.
The lower number (atomic number) counts protons; the upper number (mass number) counts protons plus neutrons.

low.restatement: Take carbon-12: symbol C, bottom number 6, top number 12. Six protons, six electrons, and 12 − 6 = 6 neutrons.
low.analogy: Nuclear notation is like a name badge with two counters — the top counter totals every heavy particle, the bottom counter identifies which element it is.
low.examPointer: Practise reading notation both ways: given the symbol, find the particle counts; given the counts, write the symbol.

medium.restatement: The atomic number fixes the element’s identity and equals both the proton count and, in a neutral atom, the electron count. The mass number totals the nucleons, so neutron number is their difference. Removing electrons changes charge but not the nuclear identity.
medium.analogy: Think of a shopping receipt: the atomic number is the store name (never changes), the mass number is the item count, and the neutrons are the receipt total minus the store line.
medium.examPointer: Ionisation questions hinge on electrons only — removing electrons never alters the mass number.

check.stem: In nuclear notation, which number is written at the top of the symbol?

options.text: the mass number
options.explanation: The mass number (protons + neutrons) sits above the symbol.

options.text: the atomic number
options.explanation: The atomic number is written below the symbol.

options.text: the number of electrons
options.explanation: Electrons are not shown in nuclear notation.

options.text: the charge of the nucleus
options.explanation: The notation shows particle counts, not charge.

check.stem: An atom loses two electrons. What happens to its nuclear notation numbers?

options.text: both numbers stay the same; only the charge changes
options.explanation: Electron loss changes the ion’s charge but not the proton or nucleon counts.

options.text: the mass number falls by 2
options.explanation: Electron mass is negligible — the mass number is unchanged.

options.text: the atomic number falls by 2
options.explanation: Protons define the atomic number and are unaffected by electron loss.

options.text: the atom becomes a different element
options.explanation: Element identity follows the proton count, which has not changed.

check.stem: A neutral atom has atomic number 8. How many electrons orbit it?

options.explanation: In a neutral atom the electron count equals the proton count, which is the atomic number.
That would double the count for no reason.

options.text: 8 nucleons minus the electrons
options.explanation: Electrons are not subtracted from nucleons.

options.text: it cannot be known without the mass number
options.explanation: Neutrality fixes electrons from the atomic number alone.

check.stem: What does the difference (mass number − atomic number) give?

options.text: the number of neutrons
options.explanation: Mass number totals nucleons; subtracting protons leaves neutrons.

options.text: the number of protons
options.explanation: Protons are given by the atomic number itself.

options.text: the number of electrons
options.explanation: Electrons equal protons in a neutral atom, not the difference.

options.text: the total charge
options.explanation: A neutral atom’s total charge is zero regardless of this difference.

check.stem: Why is an ion of an element still that same element?

options.text: because its atomic number, set by its protons, is unchanged
options.explanation: Element identity depends only on the proton count.

options.text: because the number of neutrons stayed the same
options.explanation: Neutrons distinguish isotopes, not elements.

options.text: because the mass number is unchanged
options.explanation: Mass number separates isotopes; identity is proton-based.

options.text: because electrons always return to the atom
options.explanation: Ions can persist; identity never depended on them.

check.stem: Define the term atomic number.
check.modelAnswer: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; it also equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom.

check.stem: Write the nuclear notation description for an atom of sodium, atomic number 11 and mass number 23, and state its neutron count.
check.modelAnswer: Sodium is written with mass number 23 above and atomic number 11 below the symbol Na; its neutrons number 23 − 11 = 12.

check.stem: Explain why removing electrons from an atom does not change its nuclear notation numbers.
check.modelAnswer: The mass number counts protons and neutrons only, and the atomic number counts protons only; electrons carry negligible mass and are not counted, so removing them alters neither number.

check.stem: Use nuclear notation for uranium: atomic number 92, mass number 238. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom.
check.modelAnswer: Protons = atomic number = 92; neutrons = 238 − 92 = 146; electrons = protons = 92 in the neutral atom.

lessons.title: Atomic and mass numbers
lessons.opening: The atomic number is the proton count that fixes which element an atom belongs to, while the mass number totals the nucleons in the nucleus. Between them they determine the neutron count, because neutrons equal mass number minus atomic number.
keyPoints: The atomic number (proton number) is fixed for every atom of a given element.
The periodic table orders the elements by atomic number.
The mass number (nucleon number) is the total of protons and neutrons.
Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
In a neutral atom the electron count equals the atomic number.

low.restatement: Sodium: atomic number 11, mass number 23. That is 11 protons, 11 electrons, and 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons.
low.analogy: The atomic number is your surname (fixed by family), the mass number is the size of your whole household.
low.examPointer: A one-mark staple: subtract to find neutrons. Write the subtraction explicitly to earn the working mark.

medium.restatement: Because the proton count defines the element, changing it means a different element appears — the basis of transmutation in decay. The nucleon total can vary between isotopes of one element without changing identity.
medium.analogy: Changing the atomic number re-brands the element entirely, like changing the country on a passport; changing the mass number only swaps the passport’s edition.
medium.examPointer: Exam tables often give two of {protons, neutrons, mass number} — fill the third with atomic number = protons and mass = protons + neutrons.

check.stem: What determines which element an atom is?

options.text: the number of protons in its nucleus
options.explanation: The atomic (proton) number fixes the element.

options.text: the number of neutrons
options.explanation: Neutrons vary between isotopes of the same element.

options.text: the number of electrons
options.explanation: Electrons can be lost to ionisation without changing the element.

options.text: its total mass in kilograms
options.explanation: Identity is a particle count, not a measured mass.

check.stem: A chlorine atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. How many neutrons does it contain?

options.explanation: Neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18.
17 is the proton count, not the difference.
35 is the mass number, the total of protons and neutrons.
That adds the numbers instead of subtracting.

check.stem: Which statement about the mass number is correct?

options.text: it is the total number of protons and neutrons
options.explanation: Mass number counts all nucleons.

options.text: it is the number of protons only
options.explanation: That is the atomic number.

options.text: it includes the electrons
options.explanation: Electron mass is negligible and excluded.

options.text: it is always equal to the atomic number
options.explanation: It exceeds the atomic number whenever neutrons are present.

check.stem: Hydrogen has atomic number 1. An atom of hydrogen-3 (tritium) contains how many neutrons?

options.explanation: Neutrons = 3 − 1 = 2.
That is the proton count of hydrogen.
3 is the mass number, not the neutron count.
Hydrogen-1 has no neutrons, but hydrogen-3 has two.

check.stem: Why do atoms of the same element always share one number, however many neutrons they carry?

options.text: because the atomic number, and so the proton count, never varies within an element
options.explanation: The proton count defines the element and is invariable.

options.text: because neutron counts never vary either
options.explanation: Neutron counts are exactly what varies between isotopes.

options.text: because mass numbers are identical for all atoms of an element
options.explanation: Mass number differs between isotopes.

options.text: because electrons adjust the nuclear count
options.explanation: Electrons are outside this counting entirely.

check.stem: Define the term mass (nucleon) number.
check.modelAnswer: The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

check.stem: Gold has atomic number 79 and mass number 197. State its numbers of protons and neutrons.
check.modelAnswer: Gold has 79 protons (its atomic number) and 197 − 79 = 118 neutrons.

check.stem: Explain why the atomic number of sodium is always 11 in every sample of sodium, worldwide.
check.modelAnswer: The atomic number is the number of protons, and an atom is only sodium if its nucleus contains exactly 11 protons; any other proton count would make it a different element.

check.stem: A neutral atom is written in nuclear notation with mass number 39 and atomic number 19. State its proton, neutron and electron counts.
check.modelAnswer: Protons = 19, neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20, and electrons = 19 because the atom is neutral.

glossary.definition: The tiny, dense centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons, holding nearly all of its mass.
An atom that has lost or gained electrons and so carries an overall charge.
The writing of an element symbol with its mass number above and atomic number below.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.

workedExample.prompt: A nucleus of carbon-12 contains 6 protons. How many electrons are there in a neutral carbon atom?
steps: The proton count of carbon is 6.
A neutral atom has equal numbers of electrons and protons.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The neutral carbon atom has 6 electrons.
